name: Mansim
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_citation: Reesink, Ger P. 2002. Mansim, a lost language of the Bird's Head. In Ger P. Reesink (ed.), Languages of the Eastern Bird's Head, 277-340. Pacific Linguistics 524. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics.
catalog_quote: 2.1 Stress If the segmental units leave many questions, this is even more the case with regard to suprasegmental features. It is possible that Mansim has a tonal difference between what I recorded as homophones. For example, the various instances of bar 'something; carry; not' and tan 'inside; far; afraid' could require different pitch, but on the basis of my restricted data, this could not be ascertained. Stress seems to be distributed according to an iambic pattern over the clause, pretty much like in Hatam. That is, person prefixes do not receive stress, nor do other first syllables in polysyllabic words, with the exception of full personal pronouns. What I identified as citation markers can be stressed, as can possessive pronouns, while major categories like nouns or verbs do not necessarily attract main stress. tone_statements.citation: Reesink, Ger P. 2002. The eastern Bird's Head languages compared. In Ger P. Reesink (ed.), Languages of the Eastern Bird's Head, 1-44. Pacific Linguistics 524. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, The Australian National University.
tone_statements.quote: Mpur clearly has phonemic tone, Meyah and Sougb a pitch-accent system. Hatam and Mansim do not have a tonal distinction, which they may well have had in the past (the number of homophones in Hatam is considerable), but Hatam does have a very pronounced iambic stress pattern over the utterance as a whole, defying attempts to determine a pattern of word stress.
tone_statements.locator: p.26, section 7.1 'Phonology' (in sec. 7 on Austronesian vs Papuan features)

audit.reasoning: Quote confirmed verbatim at p.282 sec. 2.1 in the scanned text we hold and again in the freshly downloaded original PDF. The classification (PHRASAL, domain phrase, listed-set exception for full pronouns) follows the source's wording directly, and the Hatam reference grammar the author points to (held) describes exactly a clause-domain iambic metre with no word stress. The source is the only description of Mansim that exists (Glottolog: 0 descriptive refs), so nothing better can be obtained; it is nonetheless a salvage sketch whose stress paragraph is explicitly tentative ('seems', possible unverified tone contrast), which is why I grade the record 'adequate' rather than 'well-sourced'. no reclassification, no identity issue (B already checked bora1263 = Bora, Witotoan, is unrelated; Hatam hata1243 is a distinct languoid). Optional housekeeping only: add the downloaded PDF path to the record's copies we hold.
